title: What is the cheapest payment-and-audit protocol that makes honest ML training an equilibrium?
lede: research programme: incentive-compatible verification of outsourced ML training; first measurement on real training finds a tolerance-tau referee passes a skip-steps cheat on 30% of steps at tau = 1e-2 while the held-out loss stays within one seed std, and the loss only suffers at tau about 10x the worst benign drift
summary: An open research programme rather than a finished project. A requester pays untrusted workers to train a model; cheating is cheap and the product cannot be checked without redoing the work. The programme asks for the cheapest protocol that makes full-effort training an equilibrium when the checks are a refereed re-execution of a disputed step, a noisy proper score of the final model on held-out data, and agreement among redundant workers, and when honest workers disagree by floating-point drift. It consolidates about 60 stylised projects in this repository (verification-game, audit-allocation, verifier-bribery, effort-elicitation, reproducible-refereed-training and others). Planned: the drift tolerance priced as a cheating margin, a joint contract over audit rate, stake and score with a proved cost frontier, the stake needed against workers who share one cheap trajectory, and measurement on real small-model training. First result (H1, milestone 3): on a 64-64-10 MLP trained on the real scikit-learn digits data over 20 seeds, a referee that accepts a step within L2 distance tau passes a worker that skips, subsamples or lowers precision whenever the alternative is within tau. Benign float16 drift is at most 9×10−3 (median 3×10−5); skipping passes 30% of steps at tau = 10−2 and costs less than one seed standard deviation of held-out loss, and costs 30 standard deviations only at tau = 0.1. At drift-sized tolerances the margin is saved work rather than a worse model. One dataset, one small model and plain SGD; H2 to H6 are untested.
